Looking for Student Teammates! 

Hey everyone! We're a team of students participating in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

We're working on the challenge "Be An Earth System Trend Detective"

We're hoping to connect with other  students, who are interested in space, science, coding or research and would like to work together on this challenge.

No need to be an expert just bring your curiosity and ideas!

Interested? Drop a comment or DM me.
summary: Earth in Sound lets you listen to our planet. We turn NASA Earth data and satellite images into sound in the browser, so you can hear 146 years of global temperature, the Arctic warming faster than the Tropics, the seasons of your own city, natural events NASA is tracking right now, and satellite maps played from west to east like a song. The challenge asked how people who are blind or have low vision could experience NASA's Earth Information Center visuals. Most climate information still comes as charts and maps, and if you can't see them well, the story is closed to you. Even for people who can, a number like "1.2 °C" is hard to feel. We wanted a way in that works by ear first. Every note in Earth in Sound is a real value from NASA, mapped to sound by fixed, simple rules: warmer plays higher, more rain adds more notes, brighter sunlight opens up the sound. A chart, a spoken readout and a data table show the same numbers, so it works with sound, with sight, or both. It opens on a 3D Earth made from NASA's Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery. You tap any place on the globe and hear its climate. There's no account, no app to install, and after one visit it keeps working offline, which matters to us because internet here in Bangladesh isn't always reliable.
details:
What exactly does it do?

Earth in Sound is a listening instrument for Earth data. You pick a view, press play, and hear the data change over time while the chart and readout follow along.

  • Home globe: a 3D Earth built from NASA Blue Marble and Black Marble imagery, lit by where the Sun really is right now. Spin it, tap a place, and press Listen here to hear that spot's climate.
  • Planet: NASA GISTEMP global temperature from 1880 to 2025, one note per year. You can hear the line climb. Since 1980 it rises about 0.21 °C per decade, and 2024 is the warmest year in the record.
  • Regions: three parts of the world at once, one in each ear and one in the middle, all on the same scale. Poles and Tropics, North and South, or latitude bands. With headphones you can hear the Arctic pull away. Since 1980 it has warmed about 0.66 °C per decade, roughly three times the global rate.
  • My Place: monthly temperature, rain and sunlight since 2001 for any city, from NASA POWER. 32 cities are saved in the app, including Dhaka, Chattogram, Sylhet, Khulna and Rajshahi, so they load instantly and work offline.
  • Compare: two cities, one in each ear, on one shared temperature scale. The same note means the same temperature on both sides.
  • Events: wildfires, storms, volcanoes and ice that NASA's EONET feed has tracked over the last 60 days. Fires crackle, storms drum, ice rings, and each sound sits left or right depending on where on Earth it happened.
  • Scan: a line sweeps across NASA satellite maps of air temperature, sea surface temperature and plant cover, turning each column into notes. You can also load your own image, such as a frame from the Earth Information Center, and hear its colours and brightness.
  • Take a listen: a one-minute guided tour of the planet, the poles and three years of Dhaka. The captions are worked out from the data, and they can be read aloud.
  • Range, Share, Data and Saved setups: listen to any span of years, send a link that opens the exact same setup, download the numbers as a CSV with units and sources, and keep your favourite setups on your device.

How does it work?

  1. Getting the data. A small Node.js script downloads NASA GISTEMP tables, NASA POWER monthly data for our saved cities, the EONET event feed and GIBS map images. It checks everything before saving: years in order, real numbers, expected units, no fill values like -999. It also stores where each file came from and when.
  2. Loading it in the browser. The app plays the saved data straight away, then tries the live NASA services in the background. If a request fails, it says so and tells you which saved place is playing instead.
  3. Turning numbers into sound. Each view uses one fixed scale for its whole record, so a note always means the same value even when you zoom into a shorter range. Pitch follows a C major pentatonic scale so it stays pleasant to listen to. Temperature sets pitch, rain sets how many notes fall, sunlight sets brightness, and position on Earth sets left and right. Missing values are skipped, never played as zero.
  4. Reading the maps. For Scan, we use NASA's own colour legends for each GIBS layer to read values back from the map colours, column by column, from west to east.
  5. Keeping it in sync. The chart, the slider, the spoken readout, the findings and the CSV all come from the same points as the sound, so what you hear is what you see.
  6. Working offline. A service worker saves the app, the font and all the bundled data on the first visit, so it opens and plays even without internet.

What benefits does it have?

  • Accessibility: climate data you can follow by ear. Every control works from the keyboard, has a label for screen readers, and the timeline announces the date and value as you move through it.
  • Learning: students and teachers can hear a trend instead of just being told about it, and then check the exact numbers in the Data panel.
  • Local: your own city becomes part of the story. Hearing Dhaka's monsoon next to London's flat seasons makes a difference most charts don't.
  • Honest: every source, unit, baseline and limitation is one tap away, and the app says plainly when it's using saved data instead of live data.
  • Easy to reach: free, open source, no login, works on a phone, and works on patchy internet.

What do you hope to achieve?

Right now we haven't tested Earth in Sound with blind or low-vision listeners, and that's the first thing we want to fix. In the short term, we want to sit down with blind and low-vision students, teachers and classmates, watch how they use it, and change what doesn't work for them. We also want to add Bangla so more people here can use it. Longer term, we'd like Earth in Sound to become a simple way to listen to any NASA Earth visual, so that a classroom anywhere can open a map or a chart and hear it, not just see it.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, GLSL (for the globe)
  • Frontend: Vite, Tone.js (sound), uPlot (charts), WebGL (3D globe), Web Audio API, Speech Synthesis API (spoken captions), MediaRecorder (recording), Service Worker (offline)
  • Data scripts: Node.js
  • Testing: Vitest, Playwright, Google Chrome
  • Hosting and code: GitHub, GitHub Actions, GitHub Pages, Vercel
  • Place search: Open-Meteo Geocoding API
  • Font: Manrope (SIL Open Font License, via Fontsource)
  • AI coding assistants: Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code, and Codex (OpenAI)
  • Development tools: [CONFIRM: editor, e.g. Visual Studio Code], Git, npm
  • Video: [CONFIRM: video editing software]
  • Hardware: our own laptops and phones, and headphones for listening
